claims.text: High configurational entropy synchronizes the high-temperature diffusion rates of reactive elements such as Al and Cr.
Synchronized diffusion provides a continuous, balanced supply of Al and Cr to the oxidation front.
Balanced reactive-element supply produces a thinner and more uniform protective oxide than in a lower-entropy conventional alloy.
Balanced reactive-element supply gives the protective oxide self-healing capability.
Al and Cr are oxide-forming alloying elements capable of contributing protective alumina or chromia scales.
The proposed initial alloy is equiatomic Al-Cr-Fe-Ni-Co.
The equiatomic Al-Cr-Fe-Ni-Co alloy is in a single solid-solution phase.
All elements in the initial alloy are uniformly distributed.
A lower-mixing-entropy baseline can be produced by induced segregation or phase heterogeneity while retaining identical concentrations of the oxide-forming elements.
The controlled comparison exposes both alloy variants to identical oxidation conditions between 800 °C and 1200 °C in a controlled oxygen atmosphere.
High mixing entropy prevents localized depletion of oxide-forming elements at the oxidation front.
Balanced replenishment reduces defect formation in the oxide scale.
A less defective oxide scale has improved adhesion and enhanced self-healing, thereby increasing oxidation resistance.
Under identical oxidation conditions, the high-entropy variant will form a thinner, more uniform, and less defective oxide scale than the baseline.
The lower-entropy baseline will have unbalanced diffusion rates that produce a thicker, more heterogeneous, and more defect-prone oxide scale.
The proposed synchronization mechanism operates over 800 °C to 1200 °C under controlled oxygen partial pressures.
Oxygen partial pressure materially affects high-temperature oxide growth and scale thickness.
Alternative diffusion pathways or high-temperature phase instabilities may diminish the relevance of the proposed mechanism.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in oxide thickness, improved uniformity, and lower defect density in the high-entropy variant would falsify the hypothesis.
